title: Compare and Contrast Common Social Engineering Attacks, Threats, and Vulnerabilities

sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: This objective joins three security ideas: social engineering manipulates people, threats attack systems or organizations, and vulnerabilities are weaknesses that make attacks easier.
sections.callout: Trick the person → attack the system → exploit the weakness.

sections.title: Maestro Focus
paragraphs: Identify the exact attack from the delivery channel, target, behavior, technical destination, or weakness emphasized in the scenario.
bullets: Email → phishing; voice → vishing; SMS → smishing
One source flood → DoS; distributed sources → DDoS
Database input → SQL injection; browser script → XSS
Fix exists but is absent → unpatched; vendor fixes ended → EOL

sections.title: Social Engineering
paragraphs: Social engineering attacks the human decision-maker rather than relying only on a technical exploit.

entries.title: Phishing
paragraphs: Uses fraudulent messages, usually email, to induce clicks, attachments, credential disclosure, payments, or other actions.

entries.title: Vishing
paragraphs: Voice-based phishing, often a call from someone pretending to be a bank, help desk, or vendor.

entries.title: Smishing
paragraphs: Phishing delivered through SMS or text messaging.

entries.title: QR Code Phishing
paragraphs: Uses a malicious or deceptive QR code to direct a victim to a fraudulent destination.
entries.recognitionCue: Malicious QR code → QR code phishing.

sections.title: Spear Phishing and Whaling

entries.title: Spear Phishing
paragraphs: Targets a specific person or group and uses contextual information to appear convincing.

entries.title: Whaling
paragraphs: Targets a high-value executive or senior leader.

sections.callout: Broad campaign → phishing; selected victim → spear phishing; executive victim → whaling.

entries.title: Shoulder Surfing
paragraphs: Observes someone entering a password, PIN, door code, or other sensitive information.

entries.title: Tailgating
paragraphs: Enters a restricted area by following an authorized person through a controlled door.

entries.title: Impersonation
paragraphs: Pretends to be a trusted employee, technician, manager, vendor, or organization.

entries.title: Dumpster Diving
paragraphs: Searches discarded materials for passwords, account information, internal documents, or hardware details.

entries.title: Denial of Service (DoS)
paragraphs: Overwhelms or exhausts a service from one or a limited number of sources to make it unavailable.

entries.title: Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS)
paragraphs: Uses many distributed systems to overwhelm one target.

entries.title: Evil Twin
paragraphs: A fraudulent wireless access point that imitates a legitimate network to attract users and intercept traffic.
entries.recognitionCue: Fake Wi-Fi that looks real → evil twin.

entries.title: Zero-Day Attack
paragraphs: Exploits a newly unknown or uncorrected vulnerability before an effective fix is available or defenders have meaningful response time.
entries.recognitionCue: New flaw with no ready fix → zero-day.

entries.title: Spoofing
paragraphs: Falsifies identity or source information such as an email address, IP address, caller ID, or MAC address.

entries.title: On-Path Attack
paragraphs: Places an attacker between communicating parties to read, capture, or alter traffic.

entries.title: Brute-Force Attack
paragraphs: Systematically tries many possible passwords or keys until one works.

entries.title: Dictionary Attack
paragraphs: Tries candidate passwords from a prepared word or common-password list.
entries.recognitionCue: Try a word list → dictionary attack.

sections.title: Insider and Web Threats

entries.title: Insider Threat
paragraphs: Risk created by an employee, contractor, or partner with legitimate access acting maliciously, negligently, or accidentally.
entries.recognitionCue: Danger from authorized access → insider threat.

entries.title: Structured Query Language (SQL) Injection
paragraphs: Uses malicious input to manipulate database queries.
entries.recognitionCue: Attacker input changes a database query → SQL injection.

entries.title: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)
paragraphs: Injects malicious web content that executes as script in another user's browser.
entries.recognitionCue: Web input becomes browser script → XSS.

sections.callout: Database query → SQL injection; browser-executed script → XSS.

entries.title: Business Email Compromise (BEC)
paragraphs: Uses fraudulent or compromised business email identities to request payments, change account details, or disclose sensitive data.
entries.recognitionCue: Trusted-looking corporate email requests financial action → BEC.

entries.title: Supply Chain/Pipeline Attack
paragraphs: Compromises a trusted vendor, software provider, update mechanism, dependency, or service to reach downstream customers.
entries.recognitionCue: Attack the trusted supplier to reach the customer.

sections.title: Vulnerabilities
paragraphs: A vulnerability is a weakness that can be exploited.

entries.title: Non-Compliant Systems
paragraphs: Do not meet required organizational or regulatory standards.
entries.recognitionCue: Policy requires one state; the system has another.

entries.title: Unpatched Systems
paragraphs: Are missing available security fixes.
entries.recognitionCue: A fix exists but was not installed.

entries.title: Unprotected Systems
paragraphs: Lack expected controls such as antivirus or a firewall.
entries.recognitionCue: Missing antivirus or missing firewall → unprotected.

entries.title: End-of-Life (EOL)
paragraphs: No longer receive normal vendor support or security updates.

entries.title: Bring Your Own Device (BYOD)
paragraphs: A personally owned device used for business can introduce unknown posture, mixed data, privacy concerns, unsupported software, loss risk, and limited organizational control.
entries.recognitionCue: Personal device plus business data → BYOD risk.

Personally controlled device handles business data

sections.title: Recognition Cues
bullets: Follow through a secure door → tailgating
Trusted vendor compromise → supply chain attack

sections.title: Objective 2.5 Exam Trap
bullets: Email is phishing, voice is vishing, SMS is smishing, and a malicious code image is QR code phishing.
A specific target is spear phishing; an executive target is whaling.
Shoulder surfing watches credentials; tailgating follows a person through a controlled entrance.
DoS uses one or limited sources; DDoS is distributed.
An evil twin is a fake access point; spoofing falsifies source identity.
Brute force tries broad combinations; a dictionary attack tries prepared words.
SQL injection targets database queries; XSS runs script in a browser.
A zero-day lacks an effective ready fix; an unpatched system skipped an available fix.

sections.title: Maestro Recognition Sheet
sections.callout: Trick the person → attack the system → exploit the weakness.
